sources.name: Measured ladders

options.name: (a) Affine remap: the Dynamic Boost slider's eleven positions span MIDI 0..70 instead of 0..127
options.how: Add to crates/fxsound-core/src/lib.rs scale: `pub const DYNAMIC_BOOST_MAX_MIDI: u8 = 70;` plus `slider_to_value_for(effect, slider)` and `value_to_slider_for(effect, value)`. For DynamicBoost, slider_to_value_for(p) = p * 70.0 / 10.0 / 127.0 (so value_to_midi gives exactly 7p for integer p) and value_to_slider_for(v) = (v * 127.0 / 7.0).min(10.0); for the other four they delegate to the existing functions unchanged. Route the four conversion sites through them: app.rs:459 (apply_preset), app.rs:474 (current_preset_snapshot), app.rs:615 (sync_params_from_state), and the CLI's --set_effect parse in cli.rs around :816/:1050, plus crates/fxsound-preset/examples/write_preset.rs:168. gain_boost_for_amount and maxi_boost_db in dynamic_boost.rs are NOT touched — the DSP stays bit-faithful. The resulting ladder, verified against the f32 chain: 0.00, 0.80, 1.70, 2.50, 3.50, 4.40, 5.20, 6.20, 8.00, 9.80, 11.60 dB at positions 0..10, every one distinct and monotone.
options.breaks: (1) A position number no longer means the same thing as on Windows: position 5 becomes 4.4 dB where Windows gives 10.0 dB. Community advice and docs that say 'set Dynamic Boost to 4' become approximate. (2) 22 of the 34 shipped presets currently sit exactly on a detent (stored 0, 13, 25, 38, 51, 64, 127); after the remap only the four zeros do. apply_preset does not round, so their sound is untouched on load — but one click on that slider now snaps them, changing the gain by at most 0.4 dB (stored 25 -> 28 is 3.10 -> 3.50 dB; stored 51 -> 49 is 6.60 -> 6.20 dB). Today that same click is near-lossless. (3) A preset saved on Linux at position 10 stores 70; reopened on Windows it shows '6' (70/12.7 = 5.51, JUCE snaps to 6) and, if re-saved there, stores 76. Both produce +11.60 dB, so the file drifts but the sound does not. (4) The two tests at dynamic_boost.rs:540-573 and the round-trip report at shipped_presets.rs:287-305 must be re-expressed against the new per-effect map. (5) The .fac parser and writer are untouched, so the byte-for-byte round-trip contract itself is unaffected — what changes is only which value the app chooses to store when the user moves that one slider.
options.why: It is the only option that makes all eleven positions audibly distinct without touching a single number the DSP consumes. Every stored value still maps to exactly the gain the Windows build gives it, so no preset — shipped or imported — changes how it sounds. The mapping is one affine constant, not a magic table, and it lives in the UI layer where the defect actually is.

options.name: (b) Leave the mapping; mark the ceiling in the interface
options.how: In crates/fxsound-ui/src/views/pro.rs:264-277, draw the Dynamic Boost readout in the muted colour once the stored value is at or past the saturation point, or replace the '{value:.0}' readout with the achieved dB from a new pub fn gain_boost_db_for_amount() exported from dynamic_boost.rs. Optionally stop the slider's track fill at the saturation point. No change to fxsound-core, no change to what is stored.
options.breaks: Nothing. The 34 shipped presets, imported Windows presets, the CLI, the .fac round trip and both existing DSP tests all stay exactly as they are.
options.why: Zero risk and it stops the app lying, but the user is still handed a control whose top five positions do nothing — the complaint is not addressed, only labelled. Worth doing as a companion to (a): showing '+9.8 dB' next to the thumb makes the whole stage legible, and (a) plus the dB readout is the complete fix.

options.name: (c) Change the warp — drop or reduce the 1.8, or reorder the clamp so it applies after the 0.7 scale
options.how: Edit MUSIC2_BOOST_FACTOR at crates/fxsound-dsp/src/effects/dynamic_boost.rs:116, or move the .min(127) from line 343 to after line 344 so the index can reach 127 and the table's 12..30 dB region opens up.
options.breaks: Every preset ever made, on both platforms. Dropping the warp turns stored 51 from 6.60 dB into 5.00 dB and stored 127 from 11.60 dB into 11.60 dB (the 0.7 scale still caps at index 88) — so it does not even remove the ceiling. Moving the clamp is worse: stored 127 would jump from +11.60 dB to +30.00 dB of auto-gain into a limiter whose ceiling is -0.3 dBFS, which is not a louder preset, it is a pumping one. The four Quizal presets and every Windows preset storing 127 would be unrecognisable. The port's central claim dies.
options.why: This is the one change the port's compatibility contract explicitly forbids, and it does not even buy what it costs: the 0.7 scale, not the 1.8 warp, is what caps the effect at +11.60 dB. Removing the warp only re-spreads the slider downward while still ending at the same ceiling.

options.name: (d) dB-even detents: an eleven-entry lookup table chosen so each position is ~1.16 dB above the last
options.how: Same plumbing as (a), but instead of an affine map use a const table BOOST_DETENTS: [u8; 11] = [0, 10, 19, 28, 37, 47, 52, 57, 61, 66, 70], found by searching the f32-faithful chain for the MIDI value nearest each k*11.6/10 target. Ladder: 0.0, 1.2, 2.3, 3.5, 4.6, 5.8, 7.0, 8.2, 9.2, 10.4, 11.6 dB — steps of 1.0 to 1.2 dB throughout.
options.breaks: Everything (a) breaks, and more of it. The inverse map is a binary search rather than a division. Position 5 becomes 5.8 dB against Windows' 10.0 dB, the largest divergence of any option. And 30 of the 34 shipped presets land between detents instead of (a)'s 30 — no better — while the table has to be justified entry by entry rather than derived from one constant.
options.why: Genuinely the most even control, and if the goal were a well-tempered fader this would win. It loses to (a) on explainability and on how far it moves the meaning of a position number, for a gain in evenness that matters mostly at the top where the table's own slope doubles anyway.

options.name: (e) Conservative piecewise remap: keep positions 0..5 exactly where they are, redistribute only the dead top
options.how: A table again, but [0, 13, 25, 38, 51, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 70] — the first six entries are precisely what value_to_midi produces today. Ladder: 0.0, 1.6, 3.1, 4.7, 6.6, 10.0, 10.2, 10.4, 10.8, 11.0, 11.6 dB.
options.breaks: Almost nothing. All 22 shipped presets that sit on a detent today still do. Positions 0..5 are bit-identical to Windows. The only visible change: presets storing 76, 89, 102 or 114 stop displaying as 6, 7, 8, 9 and all display as 10 — which is honest, since they are all the same sound. Saving such a preset rewrites it to 70, again with no change in gain.
options.why: Maximum compatibility and it does make every position distinct. But positions 6..10 span 1.4 dB in total, in steps of 0.2 to 0.4 dB on a slow auto-gain stage — below what anyone will hear. It converts 'half the slider does nothing' into 'half the slider does almost nothing with a moving number', which is more honest but not much more useful. Take it if position-number compatibility with the Windows build is judged a hard requirement.

options.name: (f) Raise PLY_OPTIMIZER_BOOST_MAX_SCALE above 0.7 to unlock the table's 12..30 dB region
options.how: Change BOOST_MAX_SCALE at crates/fxsound-dsp/src/effects/dynamic_boost.rs:119.
options.breaks: The gain for every non-zero stored value on every preset, immediately and by a lot.
options.why: The 0.7 is the one part of this chain that reads as deliberate — it is the safety cap that keeps a user from asking a limiter for 30 dB of makeup. Listed only so it is on the record as considered and refused.

found.recommendation:
Do (a) plus the readout half of (b), and fix one number in the spec.

**First, the finding that decides the whole question: this is an inherited defect, not a port defect.** The Windows GUI's Dynamic Boost slider spans the full MIDI range. `FxAudioControls.cpp:113` is `setRange(0, 10, 1.0)` for all five effect sliders with no per-effect case; `valueChanged` at `:232-248` passes 0..10 to `FxController::setEffectValue`; `DfxDspPrivate.cpp:254-303` divides by 10 and hands a realtype 0..1 to `dfxpSetKnobValue`; `qntRToICalc` (`Qntrtoi.cpp:96-97`) is plain linear `(int)(x*scale + 0.5)` over `MIDI_MIN_VALUE..MIDI_MAX_VALUE`. The shipping Windows app has exactly the same dead top of the slider. The port is correct and `gain_boost_for_amount` should not be touched.

**Why it saturates, precisely.** Two independent ceilings, not one.
- `PLY_OPTIMIZER_BOOST_MAX_SCALE = 0.7` (`c_play.h:90`) applied at `dfxpComm.cpp:742` caps the table index at `(int)(127 * 0.7) = 88`, which is `+11.60 dB`. The table's 12..30 dB region (indices 90..127) is unreachable by any path, warp or no warp. That cap reads as deliberate — a limiter is not meant to be asked for 30 dB of makeup.
- `DFXP_MUSIC_MODE2_DYNAMIC_BOOST_FACTOR = 1.8` applied at `dfxpComm.cpp:709-717` with the clamp at `:719-721` landing *before* the 0.7 scale is what kills the top of the control. `f32(1.8) * 70` rounds to exactly `126.0`, so saturation begins at **MIDI 70**, not 71: all 58 values from 70 to 127 (45.3% of the range) collapse onto index 88. The clamp was written to protect a 128-entry array lookup; it ended up being the operating point of half the slider. And because `dfxpGet.cpp:166-170` defaults the mode to `MUSIC2` and nothing in `fxsound/Source/` ever sets it (SPEECH's factor is also 1.8), the warp is always in force — the unwarped `MUSIC1` path is dead code in this product.

**The fix.** The defect is in the UI layer, so fix it there. Add to the `scale` module in `crates/fxsound-core/src/lib.rs`:

```
pub const DYNAMIC_BOOST_MAX_MIDI: u8 = 70;   // the last value that changes anything
pub fn slider_to_value_for(effect: Effect, slider: f32) -> f32
pub fn value_to_slider_for(effect: Effect, value: f32) -> f32
```

For `DynamicBoost`, `slider_to_value_for(p) = p * 70.0 / 10.0 / 127.0` — chosen so `value_to_midi` returns exactly `7p` for every integer position — and `value_to_slider_for(v) = (v * 127.0 / 7.0).min(10.0)`. For the other four effects both delegate to the existing `slider_to_value` / `value_to_slider`, unchanged. Then route the five conversion sites through the per-effect pair: `app.rs:459`, `app.rs:474`, `app.rs:615`, the `--set_effect` path in `cli.rs`, and `write_preset.rs:168`. Nothing in `crates/fxsound-dsp` changes except the two tests.

The slider then reads, at positions 0 through 10: **0.00, 0.80, 1.70, 2.50, 3.50, 4.40, 5.20, 6.20, 8.00, 9.80, 11.60 dB** — every position distinct, monotone, and derived from the unmodified table. Add the dB to the readout at `pro.rs:264-277` (export a `gain_boost_db_for_amount` alongside `gain_boost_for_amount`) so the stage stops being opaque; that is the part of (b) worth keeping.

**Preset compatibility is not broken, and here is the exact accounting.** The `.fac` parser and writer are untouched, so the byte-for-byte round trip stands. `gain_boost_for_amount` is untouched, so **every stored value from 0 to 127 produces exactly the gain it produces today and exactly the gain it produces on Windows.** What changes is only which value the app *writes* when the user moves that one slider.
- The 34 shipped presets: nothing happens on load. `apply_preset` does not round, so `Competitive FPS` (stored 64) keeps its 10.00 dB and simply displays at 9.1 instead of 5. Ten presets store 70 or more — 85, 85, 95, 103, 115 and the four Quizal files at 127 — and they all display at 10 and sound at +11.60 dB before and after.
- A preset imported from Windows storing 89 or 127: loads, displays at position 10, sounds at +11.60 dB. Identical to today. If the user then edits and saves it, the file records 70 instead of 89 or 127 — a different byte, the same gain, and a value the app can now actually reproduce from its own slider.
- Round-tripping back to Windows: a Linux position 10 stores 70, which Windows shows as '6' (70/12.7 = 5.51, snapped by JUCE's interval) and would re-save as 76. The number on the screen disagrees; the sound does not.
- The real cost, stated plainly: 22 of the 34 shipped presets sit exactly on a detent today and will not after the change, so a single click on that slider will nudge them by up to 0.4 dB (stored 25 -> 28 is 3.10 -> 3.50 dB; stored 51 -> 49 is 6.60 -> 6.20 dB). That is the price. Set against it, today a user who drags a saturated preset from 10 down to 6 hears nothing at all and concludes the application is broken — which is the bug being fixed.

**Tests and docs to update in the same change.** `dynamic_boost.rs:540-563` (`the_gain_boost_mapping_matches_the_shipping_slider_table`) should keep asserting the Windows table but express it in stored MIDI rather than in slider positions, so it still guards the DSP. `dynamic_boost.rs:565-573` (`sliders_six_through_ten_are_identical...`) should be rewritten to assert the property that actually matters now — that `gain_boost_for_amount` still saturates at MIDI 70 and that the UI map never emits a value at or above it — so nobody later "fixes" the clamp order. `shipped_presets.rs:287-305` should use the per-effect map. And `docs/spec/10-dsp-effects.md:346-347` says saturation starts at `midi >= 71`; the f32 rounding makes it 70, and "the top 44%" is 45.3%.

If position-number parity with the Windows GUI is judged a hard requirement by someone who owns that call, option (e) is the fallback and costs almost nothing — but be clear that it buys distinctness, not audibility, above position 5.
found.notes:
Three things I could not settle from the source and that are worth a second pair of eyes:

1. **The 0.7 is load-bearing and I left it alone deliberately.** It, not the 1.8 warp, is why +11.60 dB is the ceiling. Removing the warp entirely (a "faithful MUSIC1" mode) would re-spread the slider downward but end at the same +11.60 dB, so it fixes nothing and changes every preset. Worth recording so the next person does not rediscover it the expensive way.

2. **`gain_boost_db_for_amount` does not exist yet.** The readout half of the recommendation needs it exported from `dynamic_boost.rs`; `maxi_boost_db` is private and takes a table index, not an amount. Small addition, but it is new public API on the DSP crate.

3. **`DFXP_INIT_DYNAMIC_BOOST_MIDI_VAL` is 51** (`dfxpDefs.h:207`), which under the new map displays at position 7.3 rather than 4. If the port has a default-preset or reset-to-default path that assumes position 4, it needs the same treatment. I did not find one, but I also did not audit the settings-restore path.

Related observations, not part of this task: the same `every_effect_amount_a_preset_stores_is_one_a_slider_can_reach` test already reports eight shipped presets storing values no slider can produce (5, 20, 54, 60, 85, 95, 103, 115) — the remap does not create that problem, it inherits it. And four Quizal presets store Dynamic Boost 127, which is the most saturated value there is; whoever authored them was dragging a slider that had stopped responding six positions earlier.

options.name: Broadcaster (the deliberately large radio voice)
options.how: A ninth preset in the input set, written as a new file beside the six drafted in docs/voice-presets-research.md (and its per-value record in docs/voice-presets-research.json). Distinguish it from Podcast by processing depth, not by tone alone: HPF ~70 Hz (keep the chest), compressor 4.5:1 at -22 dB with a slow 30 ms attack and 250 ms release, makeup +10 dB, band 1 (115.7 Hz) +2.0 dB and band 6 (1360.8 Hz) -1.5 dB for the scooped broadcast midrange, band 7 (2519.8 Hz) +2.0 dB, de-esser tight at 6000 Hz / -26 dB because the presence lift exposes sibilance. It is the only preset in the set allowed to sound processed.
options.breaks: Nothing in the .fac contract — mic presets are a new path and must not be pushed through crates/fxsound-preset/src/lib.rs, whose whole job is byte-exact round-tripping of the Windows format. It does break the drafted premise that 'the moves are small, nothing exceeds ±2 dB': Broadcaster is the one preset where a user who picks it wants to hear the difference, and holding it to the same restraint as Clean Voice makes it a duplicate of Podcast. It also needs the compressor detector question settled first (research doc objection 1), because a 4.5:1 ratio means two different things under peak vs RMS.
options.why: The single most-shipped named voice profile in the market. Blue VO!CE ships 'Broadcaster 1', 'Broadcaster 2' AND 'Classic Radio Voice'; RØDECaster Pro II ships 'Broadcast' as one of only three presets; GoXLR profiles are sold as broadcast profiles; and the entire hardware lineage (dbx 286s, Aphex 230, Symetrix) is marketed as broadcast voice processing. Four independent products, and the one name that appears three times inside a single vendor's set.

options.name: Bright Voice — the missing half of the tone pair
options.how: An input preset that mirrors Warm Voice about zero rather than inventing a new shape: band 1 (115.7 Hz) -1.5 dB, band 2 (214.3 Hz) -1.0 dB, band 7 (2519.8 Hz) +1.5 dB, band 8 (4666.1 Hz) +1.5 dB, band 9 (8640.5 Hz) +1.0 dB, HPF 90 Hz, and a de-esser that must be stronger than Warm Voice's, not equal to it (5500 Hz, around -26 dB). Ship it as a declared pair with Warm Voice in the UI list so the two read as one axis.
options.breaks: The de-esser interaction is the real cost: lifting bands 8 and 9 puts energy straight into the de-esser's detection band, so the shipped de-esser threshold and the EQ gains stop being independently tunable for this one preset. It also breaks the idea that the ten EQ gains can be validated band-by-band — Bright is the preset where the summing behaviour that crates/fxsound-dsp/tests/shipped_presets.rs already measures for output presets (adjacent bands at derived Q ≈ 1.6 adding past what any band asks) matters most, so the mic analogue of that test has to exist before this ships.
options.why: Warm and bright ship as a PAIR in every product that ships either. Blue VO!CE: 'Warm and Vintage' + 'Crisp and Modern'. Shure MV7/MV7+: 'Dark' / 'Natural' / 'Bright'. RØDECaster: Tone 'Deep' / 'Medium' / 'High', and on the Pro II a 'Sparkle' macro. SteelSeries Sonar: 'Deep Voice' vs 'Balanced'. Elgato's EQ presets include a 'High Clarity' that brings a voice forward. Five products, and shipping only the warm end is the clearest asymmetry in the planned seven.

options.name: Flat / Safety Only — protection with no voicing
options.how: HPF at 75 Hz, gate off, all ten EQ bands 0.0 dB, de-esser off, compressor off (not merely gentle), makeup 0.0 dB, limiter at -3.0 dBFS. It is the only preset where the answer to 'what does this change' is 'nothing above the rumble and nothing below the ceiling'. Distinct from the drafted Studio, which still runs a 2.0:1 compressor at -18 dB with +1.5 dB makeup.
options.breaks: It makes Studio hard to justify as a separate entry — Studio and Flat differ only by one gentle compressor, which is exactly the 'two presets that are the same voicing under different names' defect the existing shipped_presets.rs test was written to catch in the output set. Pick one: either Flat replaces Studio, or Studio gains a real identity (more makeup, a real de-esser) to earn its slot. Shipping both as drafted is the duplicate case.
options.why: Recurs as a named entry in three products plus the community consensus: Shure MOTIV 'Flat', RØDECaster Pro II 'Neutral', Discord noise suppression 'None', and every OBS guide's advice to hear the raw mic before adding filters. It also matters here specifically because the input chain, unlike the output chain, has no bypass problem to work around — nothing in it is un-bypassable the way Dynamic Boost is, so a genuinely flat input preset is honest in a way a flat output preset cannot be.

options.name: Noisy Room — the suppression case, as a preset rather than only a toggle
options.how: A preset that turns RNNoise on and tightens everything around it: gate threshold raised to about -38 dB with range_db capped near -18 dB (the field the research doc already flags as missing), HPF 100 Hz, compressor ratio held low at 2.5:1 so the gain reduction does not pump the residual floor up between phrases. Requires RNNoise to become a per-preset field on InputDspParams in crates/fxsound-dsp/src/input/mod.rs, not only a global switch in the UI.
options.breaks: Two things. It breaks the one-way relationship between the UI's RNNoise toggle and the preset — once a preset can turn RNNoise on, selecting a preset changes a control the user may have set deliberately, and the UI has to show that. And it breaks preset portability across machines that lack the RNNoise model, so the loader needs a defined behaviour when the preset asks for a denoiser that is not available (degrade to the gate, and say so) rather than failing to load.
options.why: Every product ships this case, and it is the flagship feature in most of them: NVIDIA Broadcast 'Noise Removal', Krisp 'Noise Cancellation', Discord's Krisp mode, SteelSeries 'ClearCast AI Noise Cancellation', Elgato 'Voice Focus', RNNoise first in every OBS chain. The sceptical caveat is real and worth stating: every one of them ships it as a SWITCH, never as a named voice preset. So the finding is not 'add a Noisy Room voice' but 'the suppression strength has to be part of the preset, because a preset that ignores it is describing half the sound'.

options.name: Rename Discord → Voice Chat, and Laptop Mic → Small Mic
options.how: Naming only, in the preset files and in the UI list. 'Voice Chat' for the drafted Discord numbers (90 Hz, 3.0:1 at -18 dB, +4 dB makeup); 'Small Mic' for the laptop preset, whose numbers serve a headset boom and a webcam mic identically.
options.breaks: Nothing technical. It does break the discoverability argument for app names — a user looking for a Discord preset will not find one, so the description line has to carry the app names ('Discord, Teams, Zoom, in-game voice').
options.why: No comparable product names a voice profile after a destination app. They name by role ('Podcast Studio', 'Broadcast'), by tone ('Crisp and Modern', 'Bright'), or by source ('Speech', 'Acoustic Instrument'). Krisp integrates with Discord and Zoom and still ships no Discord profile. An app name also dates badly and implies a codec-specific tuning the preset does not actually have — the -3 dBFS ceiling in the draft is already the Opus/AAC headroom argument, and it applies to all of them equally.

options.name: A three-point tone family instead of scattered tonal presets
options.how: Rather than Warm Voice and Bright Voice as two of nine loose entries, express tone as an explicit ladder — Dark / Neutral / Bright — applied over whichever destination preset is loaded, i.e. a small signed EQ offset vector added to the preset's ten gains. Implemented as a second, much smaller struct alongside InputDspParams and summed at install time in crates/fxsound-dsp/src/input/mod.rs.
options.breaks: It breaks the 'a preset is a complete stored state' model that the whole project rests on for the output side, and with it any chance of a mic preset file being a single flat list of values. It also breaks the shipped-preset tests as currently conceived: you can no longer assert that a preset's audible curve equals its stored curve, because the effective curve is a sum of two stored things. And two summed EQ curves on a fixed ladder at derived Q ≈ 1.6 is exactly how you get bands that add past what either asks for.
options.why: Three vendors converged on exactly this shape — Shure Dark/Natural/Bright, RØDE Deep/Medium/High, RØDECaster Pro II's Depth/Sparkle/Punch macros over three base presets — which is strong evidence that tone-over-destination is how people actually want to navigate. But it is a UI-contract change, not a preset addition, and the port's claim is fidelity to a stored-values model. Worth doing later, not as part of shipping the input set.

options.name: Room echo / de-reverb preset
options.how: Cannot be done in the current chain. Would need a de-reverberation stage (spectral or ML) added before the EQ, which is a new effect, not a preset.
options.breaks: The chain's shape and its real-time-safety story. Any spectral de-reverb needs an FFT with a frame buffer, and the input chain's stated contract is allocation-free after construction, sized for the worst case.
options.why: The case genuinely recurs — NVIDIA 'Room Echo Removal', Krisp 'Room Echo Cancellation', Adobe Enhance, and it is the second thing every one of them advertises after noise. But it is not a preset in any of them either, and no combination of HPF, gate, EQ, de-esser and compressor removes reverb. Naming a preset 'Room Echo' when the chain cannot do it would be the same defect the output-side tests were written to catch: a preset claiming an effect it does not get.

options.name: Singing / Acoustic Instrument / Loud (the MOTIV source-type modes)
options.how: Three presets keyed to what is in front of the mic rather than to where the audio is going: Singing (no gate, gentle 2:1, no de-esser), Acoustic Instrument (flat EQ, HPF 60 Hz, no de-esser), Loud (HPF 80 Hz, hard limiter, no makeup).
options.breaks: The framing of the whole input set. Every other preset assumes speech, and a singing preset that keeps the de-esser off and the gate open is really 'Flat with a different name' — see the Flat/Studio duplicate problem.
options.why: Fails the scepticism test: 'Speech', 'Singing', 'Flat', 'Acoustic Instrument', 'Loud' appear in exactly one vendor's lineup (Shure MOTIV, across MV5/MV51/MV88), and Shure itself dropped them for the MV7/MV7+ in favour of the Dark/Natural/Bright tone slider. One vendor, and that vendor abandoned the taxonomy.

options.name: Character presets — AM Radio, Megaphone, Telephone
options.how: EQ-only novelties: brutal HPF around 300 Hz plus a low-pass the chain does not currently have, band 6/7 lifted hard, everything else flat.
options.breaks: The chain has no low-pass stage, so a convincing telephone/AM sound is not reachable — you would get a thin voice, not a canned one. Adding a low-pass to the input chain to serve a novelty is the wrong trade.
options.why: Blue VO!CE ships 'AM Radio' and Voicemod's whole 'Devices' category is megaphones and vintage radios, so the case exists in two products — but in both it lives in a separate EFFECTS section next to pitch and formant shifting, explicitly not among the broadcast presets. Blue's own guide says the two sets 'don't always match up'. It is a different product category, not a missing voice preset.

options.name: Mic-type presets — Dynamic / Condenser / Headset
options.how: Presets differing mainly in makeup_db and HPF corner: Dynamic (low output, makeup +14 dB, HPF 70 Hz), Condenser (makeup +4 dB, HPF 90 Hz), Headset (makeup +8 dB, HPF 110 Hz).
options.breaks: It conflates gain staging with voicing. Three presets whose ten EQ gains are identical and whose only real difference is one number is the duplicate-voicing defect by construction, and it multiplies the set by three for a value the user can set with one control.
options.why: The case recurs in hardware-adjacent software — RØDECaster's generic Dynamic / Condenser / RE-20 presets, GoXLR's Dynamic/Condenser/Jack selection, Wave XLR's gain and Clipguard — but in every one of those it is a HARDWARE input selection (phantom power, preamp gain, impedance), not a voice profile. On a Linux port with no control over the interface, the honest equivalent is an input-gain control plus a level meter, not three presets.

found.recommendation:
Ship ten input presets, not seven, organised on the two axes the market actually uses — destination and tone — with one repair preset and one true bypass.

Destination: **Streaming**, **Podcast**, **Voice Chat** (the drafted Discord numbers, renamed), **Broadcaster** (new).
Tone: **Warm Voice**, **Bright Voice** (new), **Clean Voice** as the neutral centre.
Repair: **Small Mic** (Laptop Mic, renamed), **Noisy Room** (new, and the reason RNNoise has to become a per-preset field).
Reference: **Flat** (new) — HPF and limiter only. Drop **Studio** or give it an identity that is not 'Flat with a compressor'; as drafted the two are the same voicing under different names, which is precisely the defect `crates/fxsound-dsp/tests/shipped_presets.rs` was written to catch on the output side.

Three of the four additions each have four or more independent vendors behind them, and all four are reachable with the chain exactly as specified — no new stages. End to end that means: write the four new presets into the same format as the six drafted in `docs/voice-presets-research.md`, with their per-value rationale and citations in `docs/voice-presets-research.json`; add `range_db` to the gate and a detector type to the compressor on `InputDspParams` in `crates/fxsound-dsp/src/input/mod.rs` first, since Noisy Room and Broadcaster are both unspecified without them; add an RNNoise field to the same struct with a defined fallback when the model is absent; and write the mic-side analogue of `shipped_presets.rs` before any of them ship, because Bright Voice is the preset where adjacent bands at the derived Q of about 1.6 will sum past what either band asks for. Keep all of this out of `crates/fxsound-preset/src/lib.rs` — the `.fac` format is the byte-exact compatibility contract with the Windows build and has no place to put a de-esser.
found.notes:
THE ACTUAL LISTS, as shipped.

Logitech Blue VO!CE (G HUB). Factory presets confirmed by name across vendor and review sources: Broadcaster 1, Broadcaster 2 ('noticeably louder and fuller'), Crisp and Modern, Warm and Vintage ('rich undertones and smooth output'), Classic Radio Voice ('crisp, higher-pitched immediacy'), AM Radio ('intentionally canned', old car stereo), Bass Boost, plus high-voice and low-voice variants. Separately, an EFFECTS tab of character voices (DJ Robot, Electrobeast, Ethereal) built from pitch/formant PRIMARY and SECONDARY VOICE, flanger/phaser, chorus. Vendor's own guide deliberately does not publish the preset list — the pitch is 'pick one and edit it, or browse the community'. Caveat: Logitech has never published a canonical list, and G HUB's set has changed across builds; the names above are each attested at least twice but the set may not be complete.

Elgato Wave Link / Wave XLR. Ships NO named voice presets. A preset is an exported .xml of a channel's whole effect stack; the content model is Elgato Marketplace plus makers (EposVox). Wave Link 2.0's answer to the preset question is one AI button, Voice Focus (with ai|coustics), sold as making any mic studio-ready. Their published EQ presets are tonal, not role-based ('High Clarity' brings a voice forward).

RØDE. RØDECaster Pro II: three presets — Neutral, Podcast Studio, Broadcast — plus three macros, Depth, Sparkle, Punch, each moving several parameters across several processors. Original RØDECaster Pro: mic-model presets (generic Dynamic, generic Condenser, specific RØDE models, Electro-Voice RE-20), then a voice-strength preset, with Tone = Deep/Medium/High and Strength = Soft/Medium/Strong. RØDE Connect and NT-USB+: no presets at all, four always-on toggles (Noise Gate, Compressor, APHEX Aural Exciter, APHEX Big Bottom).

Shure MOTIV. MV5 / MV51 / MV88: five DSP modes — Speech, Singing, Flat, Acoustic Instrument, Loud. MV7 / MV7+ dropped those for a three-point Tone slider — Dark, Natural, Bright — alongside Auto Level Mode, Real-time Denoiser, Digital Popper Stopper, 75/150 Hz high-pass, compressor, limiter, and three reverbs (Plate, Hall, Studio). The abandonment matters: the vendor with the most source-type presets moved to a tone axis.

NVIDIA Broadcast: Noise Removal, Room Echo Removal, Studio Voice. Three effects, no presets. Krisp: Noise Cancellation, Background Voice Cancellation, Room Echo Cancellation, HD Voice, accent conversion. Toggles, no presets. Discord: Noise Suppression None / Standard / Krisp, plus Echo Cancellation, Automatic Gain Control, Input Sensitivity. No tonal anything.

SteelSeries Sonar (Mic tab): ClearCast AI Noise Cancellation, a weaker Noise Reduction, Noise Gate, and a mic EQ with named curves including Deep Voice and Balanced. GoXLR: Dynamic / Condenser / Jack input selection plus user mic profiles; 'Broadcast' is a community profile name, not a factory one. Streamlabs Desktop: seven filter types and exactly two named presets in the whole product, the Expander filter's Expander and Gate modes. Voicemod Voicelab: Characters, Devices, Surroundings — a character-effects taxonomy. Adobe Podcast Enhance: no profiles, one Enhance action with a strength slider. OBS: no presets, a consensus chain (RNNoise → gate at -26/-32 dB → three-band EQ → compressor 3:1 / -18 dB / 6 ms / 60 ms → limiter at -3 dB). Hardware (dbx 286s, Aphex 230, Symetrix): no factory presets exist; named starting points live only in third-party guides, and those always split by male vs female voice.

EasyEffects, by visibility rather than download count: the community wiki lists fifteen output/speaker preset repositories against ONE input entry, jtrv's 'Masc NPR Voice + Noise Reduction'; the other commonly passed-around input preset is MateusRodCosta's 'Improved Microphone (Male voices, with Noise Reduction)'. Neither GitHub gists nor the wiki publish download counts, so no ranking is possible — the honest signal is the 15:1 output-to-input ratio, which says the Linux input-preset space is close to empty and this port has room to define it.

THREE FINDINGS THAT SURVIVE SCEPTICISM.

1. Warm and bright always ship as a pair (five products). Shipping Warm Voice alone is the clearest gap in the seven.
2. 'Broadcast' is the most-repeated single name in the market (four products, three times inside Blue VO!CE alone), and it is a processing-depth case, not a tone case — which is why Podcast does not cover it.
3. Nobody names a voice profile after a destination app. Every vendor names by role, tone, or source. 'Discord' is ours alone.

AND THREE NON-FINDINGS, stated so they do not get re-proposed. Singing / Acoustic Instrument / Loud: one vendor, who dropped them. AM Radio / Megaphone: real, but it lives in a separate character-effects section in both products that have it, and the chain has no low-pass. Mic-type presets: real, but everywhere it appears it is a hardware input selection, not a voice profile.

Finally, a cross-check against the port's own constraint set. The input chain is still almost unbuilt — `crates/fxsound-dsp/src/input/` contains only `mod.rs` and `limiter.rs`, and `InputDspParams` does not exist yet in the tree, so the two gaps the existing research already flags (missing gate `range_db`, unspecified compressor detector) are cheap to close now and expensive after presets are written against them. Nothing recommended here touches `assets/presets/` or the `.fac` path; the shipped 34 and their six checks are unaffected.

found.area: Microphone-situation coverage of the seven planned input presets (Clean Voice, Streaming, Podcast, Discord, Warm Voice, Studio, Laptop Mic) for the FxSound Linux input chain — HPF → gate → 10-band EQ → de-esser → compressor → makeup → limiter → optional RNNoise

sources.name: Jongman, A. — Phonetics of Fricatives (Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Linguistics, in press)
sources.what: The load-bearing phonetic source for the language question. States directly: 'In Polish, the CoG and spectral peak values of the frication noise are very similar for the retroflex and alveopalatal fricatives and distinctly lower than those of the dental fricatives' (citing Nowak 2006; Bukmaier & Harrington 2016). Also establishes that Polish and Mandarin both have a three-way dental/alveopalatal/retroflex sibilant contrast, versus the two-way /s/~/ʃ/ of English, and that Mandarin and Polish /ʂ/ differ substantially in CoG despite looking alike. Extracted locally with pdftotext; WebFetch could not read the PDF.

sources.name: Bukmaier, Harrington, Reubold, Kleber — Synchronic variation in the articulation and acoustics of the Polish three-way place distinction in sibilants (Interspeech 2014)
sources.what: Primary study behind the Jongman statement. Confirms /ʂ/ and /ɕ/ have overlapping centres of gravity distinct from /s/, and that the alveolopalatal CoG sits between /s/ and /ʂ/. Its own analysis band is 500–3500 Hz for the DCT work, i.e. well below where an English-tuned de-esser looks.

sources.name: Spinu, Kochetov et al. — Acoustic classification of Russian plain and palatalized sibilant fricatives (Speech Communication)
sources.what: Establishes Russian's FOUR-way voiceless sibilant contrast (/s/, /sʲ/, /ʂ/, /ɕː/), 1,431 tokens from 10 speakers, with CoG measured over a 500–10000 Hz band at fricative onset/mid/offset. Confirms the anterior-vs-posterior contrast is carried by CoG throughout frication. I could NOT retrieve the per-phoneme Hz table — the one free full-text mirror was unreachable (DNS failure).

sources.name: Do children better understand adults or themselves? An acoustic and perceptual study of the complex sibilant system of Polish (Journal of Phonetics)
sources.what: Source of the figure that Polish adult dental /s/ has a first spectral peak and CoG 'around 8000 Hz and higher', clearly separated from /ʂ/ and /ɕ/. This is the number that puts a 5500 Hz de-esser detector below, not on, the Slavic /s/.

sources.name: NHSS: A Speech and Singing Parallel Database
sources.what: Parallel corpus of the same speakers singing and speaking. Mean dynamic range 33.60 dB for singing versus 30.95 dB for speech, and greater across-utterance variation for singing. The only apples-to-apples singing/speech dynamics number I found.

sources.name: ProSoundWeb — An Examination of Bandwidth, Dynamic Range and Normal Operating Levels
sources.what: Crest factor: normal speech ~12 dB peak factor, musical material 16–20 dB. Supports the claim that a compressor threshold voiced for speech sits wrong for singing.

sources.name: PipeWire — libpipewire-module-echo-cancel
sources.what: Acoustic echo cancellation on Linux is a separate PipeWire module using the WebRTC AEC, creating its own virtual capture/playback nodes and needing the playback signal as reference. Confirms the game-voice-chat case is an integration, not a preset.

sources.name: WirePlumber — Bluetooth configuration / LC3 codec
sources.what: HFP capture codecs and rates: CVSD 8 kHz, mSBC 16 kHz, and mono LC3-SWB (HFP 1.9) succeeding mSBC. Basis for the Nyquist arithmetic that kills EQ bands and the de-esser on Bluetooth headsets.

sources.name: In-repo: /home/blackixxce/Загрузки/fxsound-app-main/fxsound-linux/docs/voice-presets-research.json
sources.what: 116 sources already gathered. Reused rather than re-derived: proximity effect worth up to +16 dB and untrackable by a fixed preset; HFP/mSBC 16 kHz capture already noted as killing bands 8–9; WebRTC 2nd-order HPF measured -3.54 dB @100 Hz, -6.21 @80 Hz, -1.01 @150 Hz; the Discord cascade giving -7.1 dB @100 Hz; band spans at Q=1.5976 (band 1 = 85–157 Hz, band 2 = 157–292 Hz); 5 of 9 community presets put RNNoise FIRST and none put it after the limiter; the missing gate range_db and unspecified compressor detector.

options.name: Conference / several people at one microphone
options.how: New preset. The seven all assume one talker at a roughly known distance; this is the only case where the chain must level BETWEEN talkers rather than within a phrase. Inverse-square alone gives 6 dB per doubling of distance, so a near talker at 30 cm and a far one at 120 cm differ by 12 dB, and cardioid off-axis rolloff pushes the realistic spread to 15–20 dB. Concretely versus Clean Voice: HPF up to 110 Hz (no proximity effect to preserve, and the reverberant field brings more HVAC and room rumble relative to voice); gate OFF, not merely raised — a gate thresholded for the near talker removes the far talker's speech entirely, which is the classic conference failure; compressor -30 dB / 4:1 with attack 20 ms and release 600 ms so it behaves as an auto-leveller across turns instead of pumping within a sentence; makeup +10 dB to recover the lower average; EQ leaning harder on the reverberant mud and buying back lost intelligibility — 214.311 Hz -2.0, 396.85 Hz -2.5, 2519.84 Hz +2.5. The 2519.84 band matters more here than anywhere else because distance is what costs consonant intelligibility.
options.breaks: Nothing in the format. It does break the implicit assumption behind the shared gate settings (-42 to -48 dB, 2.0:1 in six of seven presets) that a gate is always appropriate, and it is the second preset after Studio to ship with the gate off — which makes the missing range_db field more visible, not less.
options.why: Genuinely distinct and completely uncovered. Every one of the seven is a single-talker preset; none of them levels across talkers, and the one stage that would try (the gate) actively destroys the case. The research JSON has exactly one hit for 'conference' across 116 sources, so this was never considered.

options.name: Headset boom mic at 2–5 cm (close-mic) as distinct from the desk case
options.how: New preset. The existing research already concedes the decisive number: proximity effect is worth up to +16 dB and 'no fixed preset can track it' — which is an argument for splitting the distance case, not for ignoring it, because +16 dB is roughly eight times the ±2 dB the seven presets actually move. Versus the desk-voiced defaults: HPF to 110–120 Hz and 4th order rather than 2nd (the general case chose 2nd order to protect the male fundamental at 80 Hz; at a 120 Hz corner on a mouth-adjacent capsule that concern inverts, and plosive energy at 2–5 cm without a pop filter runs 10–20 dB above speech and lands below 150 Hz); band 1 (115.734 Hz, span 85–157 Hz — the research calls it 'the only genuinely effective LF control in the chain') at -2.5 dB; band 2 (214.311 Hz) at -1.5; de-esser threshold ~4 dB lower than Clean Voice because a capsule at 2–5 cm captures far more sibilant and breath energy; gate threshold can safely go UP to -38 dB since the wanted signal is much hotter relative to the room.
options.breaks: Makes the desk assumption explicit, which means Clean Voice, Podcast and Warm Voice should be documented as desk-distance presets rather than universal. Nothing in the file format or the UI contract changes.
options.why: The largest single acoustic variable in the whole input problem, and the seven were, as the brief says, all voiced around the desk case. A 16 dB LF swing dwarfs every EQ move in the draft table, so no amount of re-tuning within one preset can straddle both distances.

options.name: Narrowband / Bluetooth-headset capture (the gap that was not on the list)
options.how: New preset plus a runtime guard. HFP capture is 8 kHz with CVSD and 16 kHz with mSBC; even LC3-SWB on HFP 1.9 is 32 kHz mono. Computed against the fixed ladder: at 16 kHz capture, bands 8 (8640.48) and 9 (16000) are at or above Nyquist and do nothing; at 8 kHz capture, bands 7 (4666.12), 8 and 9 are dead AND the de-esser detector at 5500–6000 Hz is above Nyquist, so the de-esser is inert in five of the seven presets; even at 32 kHz band 9 sits exactly at Nyquist. The preset: put the presence lift on 1360.79 (+1.5) and 2519.84 (+2.0) where there is still signal, leave 4666.12 and up at 0.0, move the de-esser detector down to 3800 Hz or disable it, compensate the codec's own AGC by dropping makeup to +3 dB, and raise the HPF to 120 Hz since HFP links are noisy below that anyway. The guard: read the capture node's rate and, when Nyquist falls below a band centre, grey that band out in the UI rather than letting the user spend a move on a phantom control.
options.breaks: The guard is the only real break — it makes the EQ UI rate-dependent, so the ten-band widget can no longer assume all ten are always live. The preset itself breaks nothing.
options.why: This was not in the brief's list and is the most concretely broken case I found: on a Bluetooth headset, between two and four of ten EQ bands and possibly the entire de-esser do literally nothing, and these are exactly the users with the worst microphones and the least ability to diagnose it. The research JSON already noticed the 16 kHz fact twice but only as a warning against boosting band 9 — nobody carried it through to the de-esser or to the UI.

options.name: Noisy room (fan, keyboard, traffic, family)
options.how: Would be a preset raising the gate threshold to track a floor ~20 dB higher. Do not do this. A gate is a time-domain switch: it does nothing about noise DURING speech, which is the actual complaint, and it degrades sharply as the floor rises. With the floor at -50 dB a -45 dB threshold works; move the floor to -30 dB and the threshold must climb to about -25 dB, which is roughly 10 dB below conversational peaks — close enough that it chatters on every word onset and clips the tails of quiet sentence-final syllables. The correct response is the RNNoise switch plus two parameter-set fixes the existing reviewers already raised: move RNNoise from after the limiter to FIRST, before the gate (5 of 9 surveyed community presets put denoise first, none put it after the limiter, and putting it first is what makes a fixed gate threshold meaningful because the gate then sees a cleaned floor), and add the missing range_db so the gate attenuates by a bounded -12 to -16 dB instead of to silence.
options.breaks: Moving RNNoise ahead of the limiter changes the stage order that the draft presets were all voiced against, and re-voicing is needed because every gate threshold in the table was chosen against an un-denoised floor. Adding range_db grows InputDspParams.
options.why: Rejected as a preset, kept as a real defect. It is the brief's own question answered against the preset: a 'Noisy Room' preset would ship the exact failure mode — a high gate threshold — as if it were the fix. The gain lives in stage order and a missing field, not in a row of numbers.

options.name: Language-specific sibilance (Russian, Polish) as a named preset
options.how: Would be a preset with a shifted de-esser. The phonetic evidence is real and it does not point at a preset. English has a two-way /s/~/ʃ/ contrast; Polish has three (dental /s/, retroflex /ʂ/, alveolo-palatal /ɕ/) and Russian four (/s/, /sʲ/, /ʂ/, /ɕː/). Jongman states that in Polish the retroflex and alveopalatal sit together with CoG and spectral peak distinctly LOWER than the dental, and Polish adult /s/ is reported with a first peak and CoG around 8000 Hz and above. So Slavic sibilant energy is bimodal, and a single-band detector at 5500–6000 Hz sits in the valley between the two modes: too low to sit on the Slavic /s/ it is supposed to tame, too high to touch /ʂ/ (ш, sz) — and chasing /ʂ/ downward would duck 2.5–4 kHz, the consonant intelligibility core, which is the one region every preset in the draft table BOOSTS. The right change is one number, not a preset: treat the de-esser detector frequency as a first-class per-preset parameter (it already varies 5500/6000 in the draft) and raise the default toward 7000–7500 Hz, which serves a high English /s/ and a Slavic /s/ both, while leaving the retroflex alone deliberately rather than by accident.
options.breaks: Raising the detector makes the existing de-esser thresholds slightly conservative — less energy reaches the detector, so the -22 to -25 dB thresholds will produce less reduction and want revisiting. Nothing in the format breaks.
options.why: Reject the preset, accept the finding. Users do not self-identify by sibilant inventory and will never pick a 'Russian' preset, but the underlying observation is sound and cheap to act on. Honest limit: I confirmed the Polish claim from an authoritative source and confirmed Russian's four-way contrast and CoG methodology, but I could NOT retrieve per-phoneme Hz values for Russian — the one free full-text mirror was unreachable. Treat the 7000–7500 Hz figure as inferred from the Polish numbers, not measured for Russian.

options.name: Game voice chat with the game loud in the room
options.how: Would be a preset. It cannot work. The dominant problem is acoustic echo — game audio leaving the speakers and re-entering the microphone — and removing it requires an adaptive filter fed with the playback signal as a reference. No combination of HPF, gate, EQ, de-esser and compressor has access to that reference, so no preset can address it. On Linux the answer is libpipewire-module-echo-cancel with the WebRTC AEC. Worth naming as an architectural opportunity rather than a preset: FxSound Linux already owns both the playback and the capture path, so it is unusually well placed to wire the reference up. Secondary point: most gamers wear headphones, in which case there is no echo at all and the case collapses into Discord plus keyboard clatter — which is the RNNoise row above, not a new preset.
options.breaks: An AEC integration would break the current assumption that the input path is independent of the output path, and it adds a hard dependency on the playback stream being routed through the app.
options.why: Rejected as a preset because it is categorically not a preset-shaped problem. Kept visible because it is the one case where the port has a structural advantage over a standalone plugin chain and could eventually do something no EasyEffects preset can.

options.name: Singing rather than speaking
options.how: Mostly already shipped as Studio. Studio is HPF 75 Hz, gate off, -18 dB 2.0:1 with 25/200 ms, makeup +1.5, de-esser off — which is very nearly what singing wants, and the gate being off is the single most important thing (a gate is actively harmful on sustained notes and decays, which is why the brief was right to ask). Singing's measured dynamic range is 33.60 dB against 30.95 dB for speech, and crest factor runs 16–20 dB against ~12 dB for speech, so the remaining honest deltas are a slower release (400 ms rather than 200) and ratio staying at 2.0:1. The ONE thing no speech preset can give: the HPF. Speech fundamentals floor at about 85 Hz, which is why 75–80 Hz is safe everywhere in the draft — but sung fundamentals go lower, to E2 at 82.4 Hz for a bass and C2 at 65.4 Hz for a basso profondo. Studio's 75 Hz corner therefore cuts a bass singer's fundamental, and Studio is precisely the preset a singer will reach for. Fix is a 40 Hz corner (or off) on a Studio variant, not a new preset family.
options.breaks: Dropping the corner to 40 Hz lets desk rumble and HVAC back into the compressor detector and eats limiter headroom — acceptable in a preset that already has the gate and de-esser off and is explicitly the least-processing option, unacceptable as a general default.
options.why: Genuinely distinct in exactly one parameter and identical to Studio in the rest, so it fails the brief's own test for a separate preset — but the bass-fundamental finding is real and currently mis-served, and it is a one-number fix to an existing preset.

options.name: Recording for later editing versus live
options.how: Already shipped as Studio in its EQ and dynamics — gate off, de-esser off, 2:1, flat EQ, +1.5 makeup is exactly 'the least processing that still captures cleanly'. But two numbers are wrong for the recording case and right for every other preset, which is worth correcting rather than duplicating. First, the -3.0 dBFS ceiling: the draft justifies it because the output is re-encoded by a lossy codec (Opus for Discord, AAC for streaming) that overshoots the sample peak it was given. A recording path is not lossy-encoded — it lands in WAV or FLAC in Ardour, Reaper or Audacity — so the justification does not apply and the limiter should be a safety catch at -1.0 dBFS rather than a working ceiling at -3.0. Second, makeup +1.5 dB: an editor doing their own gain staging wants the capture untouched, so 0.0 dB is the honest value.
options.breaks: Breaks the current clean claim that all presets share a -3.0 dBFS ceiling — the doc's third headline finding would need a stated exception. That is a documentation cost, not a compatibility one.
options.why: Distinct in intent and already served in substance; the delta is two numbers on an existing preset, not a new one. Rejecting it as a preset while fixing the two numbers is the correct trade.

options.name: Voice pitch: deep male ~85–100 Hz against high ~200–250 Hz
options.how: No preset. The existing research already settled this with measured numbers rather than assumption, and I found nothing to contradict it. Male F0 runs 85–180 Hz and female 165–255 Hz; the 80 Hz corner in Clean Voice and Podcast sits deliberately below the male floor, and the band spans at Q=1.5976 put band 1 (85–157 Hz) on the male fundamental and band 2 (157–292 Hz) on the female, which is why the draft sets band 0 to exactly 0.0 dB everywhere. The one genuine pitch failure is already logged as an objection: Streaming at 100 Hz and Discord at 90 Hz cascade with the VoIP stack's own 2nd-order 100 Hz Butterworth (WebRTC's measured -3.54 dB @100 Hz), giving about -7.1 dB at 100 Hz on a deep male voice.
options.breaks: Nothing — this is a no-op recommendation.
options.why: Rejected because a fixed 80 Hz high-pass demonstrably serves both pitch classes, and because users cannot self-identify by fundamental frequency anyway. The residual problem is a per-preset corner already on the objection list, not a missing situation.

found.recommendation:
Add three presets, fix four numbers, and add one runtime guard — do not add a preset for the other five cases.

Ship three genuinely new presets. **Conference** is the only one that levels between talkers rather than within a phrase: gate off, compressor -30 dB / 4:1 with a 600 ms release, HPF 110 Hz, makeup +10 dB, and a harder mud cut with 2519.84 Hz at +2.5 to buy back the intelligibility that distance costs. **Headset** splits the close-mic case off from the desk case that all seven were voiced around, because proximity effect is worth up to +16 dB and no single preset can straddle a swing eight times larger than any EQ move in the draft table: HPF 120 Hz at 4th order, band 1 at -2.5 dB, de-esser threshold 4 dB lower, gate threshold raised to -38 dB. **Narrowband** covers Bluetooth headsets, and is the case nobody had on the list: keep the presence lift on 1360.79 and 2519.84, leave everything from 4666.12 up at 0.0, drop the de-esser detector to 3800 Hz, makeup +3 dB.

Pair Narrowband with the one guard worth building: read the capture node's rate and grey out any EQ band whose centre is at or above Nyquist. The arithmetic is not marginal — at 16 kHz capture, bands 8 and 9 are dead; at 8 kHz, bands 7, 8 and 9 are dead and the de-esser detector at 5500–6000 Hz is above Nyquist, so the de-esser is silently inert in five of the seven presets. Users on the worst microphones currently get phantom controls.

Then four number changes on presets that already exist, instead of four presets that would duplicate them. Raise the de-esser detector default toward 7000–7500 Hz: Jongman's Polish data puts dental /s/ around 8000 Hz and the retroflex and alveolo-palatal distinctly lower, so a 5500 Hz detector sits in the valley between the two Slavic modes and chasing the retroflex downward would duck the 2.5–4 kHz region every preset deliberately boosts. Give Studio a variant with the HPF at 40 Hz, because sung fundamentals reach E2 at 82.4 Hz and a bass reaches C2 at 65.4 Hz, while Studio's 75 Hz corner is the preset a singer will actually reach for. Set Studio's ceiling to -1.0 dBFS and its makeup to 0.0 dB, since the -3.0 dBFS rationale is lossy-codec overshoot and a recording path is not lossy-encoded.

Finally, act on the noisy-room case as stage order rather than as a preset: move RNNoise from after the limiter to first, ahead of the gate, and add the missing gate `range_db`. This was already raised by the existing reviewers and the noisy-room analysis independently lands on it — a preset that merely raises the gate threshold would ship the failure mode as the fix. Note this forces re-voicing of every gate threshold in the draft table, since all of them were chosen against an un-denoised floor.
found.notes:
Where the evidence is thinner than it looks. The Russian sibilance conclusion is INFERRED, not measured: I confirmed Russian's four-way contrast and the CoG methodology from Spinu & Kochetov, and confirmed the Polish claim from an authoritative encyclopedia chapter, but the one free full-text mirror carrying per-phoneme Hz values for Russian was unreachable (DNS failure). The 7000–7500 Hz detector figure is extrapolated from Polish. If that number is going to be defended in a shipped preset, someone should retrieve the Kochetov table properly or measure a few Russian speakers directly. Everything else here is either from a retrieved source or arithmetic I ran.

Two source-quality notes. Both phonetics PDFs defeated WebFetch (it reported them as corrupted binary); `pdftotext` read them fine from the locally saved copies, so that is the route for any follow-up. And the singing crest-factor comparison leans on a general speech-versus-music figure (~12 dB against 16–20 dB) rather than a singing-specific one; only the 33.60 vs 30.95 dB dynamic-range pair is a true parallel measurement of the same speakers.

Relevant files. The prior research is at /home/blackixxce/Загрузки/fxsound-app-main/fxsound-linux/docs/voice-presets-research.md and its machine-readable record at /home/blackixxce/Загрузки/fxsound-app-main/fxsound-linux/docs/voice-presets-research.json — I reused its proximity, WebRTC high-pass, band-span and RNNoise-ordering findings rather than re-deriving them, as instructed. Note the draft table there lists SIX presets, not the seven in the brief: Laptop Mic has no row and no reviewed numbers, and Warm Voice is flagged as never reviewed at all. So of the seven named, two are less settled than the framing suggests.

Implementation reality check: the input chain does not exist in code yet. /home/blackixxce/Загрузки/fxsound-app-main/fxsound-linux/crates/fxsound-dsp/src/effects/ contains only the output effects (ambience, bass, dynamic_boost, fidelity, surround), and /home/blackixxce/Загрузки/fxsound-app-main/fxsound-linux/crates/fxsound-preset/src/lib.rs is the .fac output-preset parser only. `InputDspParams` is not written yet. That is good news for the two parameter-set gaps — the compressor's unspecified detector and the gate's missing `range_db` — since both can be designed in rather than retrofitted, and my Narrowband and Conference recommendations both assume the gate can be genuinely disabled per preset rather than merely thresholded away. The .fac byte-for-byte round-trip contract is not at risk from any of this: input presets are a new format and touch none of it.

One thing I deliberately did not do: the brief asked which situations the seven serve badly, and five of my nine answers are "not a preset". That is the finding, not an evasion — three of those five (RNNoise ordering, the de-esser detector, the AEC reference) are places where the preset layer is the wrong layer, and shipping presets for them would encode the bug as a product feature.

found.area: Objective measurement of genre-preset voicing: what can actually be measured through the real engine, what reference data exists as numbers, which corpora are licence-clean for this AGPL repo, and where the measurable ends

sources.name: Pestana, Ma, Reiss, Barbosa, Black — "Spectral Characteristics of Popular Commercial Recordings 1950–2010" (AES 135, paper 8960)
sources.what: The canonical genre/era spectral corpus work (~800 number-one singles). Headline result is published as text and figures — 'a consistent linear decay of about 5 dB per octave from 100 to 4000 Hz'. The per-genre curves exist only as plots behind the AES paywall. NOT available as numbers.

sources.name: Ma, Reiss, Black — "Implementation of an intelligent equalization tool using Yule-Walker for music mixing and mastering" (AES 134)
sources.what: Derives a mastering target curve from the same corpus. Same access problem; a third-party MATLAB reimplementation exists (github.com/bombsandbottles/Intelligent-Equalization) but carries the author's own curve, not the published one.

sources.name: Elowsson & Friberg — "Long-term Average Spectrum in Popular Music and its Relation to the Level of the Percussion" (AES 142, 2017)
sources.what: The single most important source for the ceiling argument: LTAS variation between genres is mainly a side-effect of percussive prominence, not of genre-specific tonal intent. Constrains how much a per-genre reference curve can ever prove.

sources.name: AcousticBrainz data dumps (2022-06-23, final)
sources.what: 29,460,584 submissions, still downloadable. Low-level CSV feature dumps are 1 GB (lowlevel), 1 GB (rhythm), 843 MB (tonal) zstd; full JSON dumps in 30 archives. Data is CC0. Contains per-track barkbands (27), melbands (40), erbbands (40) energies with mean/var statistics — the only per-track spectral summary of *commercial* masters that is downloadable as numbers under a licence this repo can vendor.

sources.name: Essentia MusicExtractor descriptor reference
sources.what: Defines what is in an AcousticBrainz lowlevel record: barkbands = spectral energy in 27 Bark bands, plus crest/flatness/skewness/spread. Confirms barkbands.mean is usable as a coarse per-track LTAS.

sources.name: FMA: A Dataset For Music Analysis (Defferrard et al., ISMIR 2017) + repository
sources.what: 106,574 CC-licensed tracks, 16,341 artists, 161-genre hierarchy. Subsets: small 8k/7.2 GiB (8 balanced genres), medium 25k/22 GiB (16 genres), large 106k/93 GiB (30 s clips), full 879 GiB. MP3, mostly 44.1 kHz stereo, 320 kbit/s nominal (263 average). Metadata is CC BY 4.0; audio is per-artist CC, and tracks.csv carries a per-track `license` column.

sources.name: MTG-Jamendo dataset
sources.what: 55k full tracks, 3,777 hours, 320 kbit/s, 87 genre tags. Audio is CC; code Apache-2.0; but METADATA IS CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — cannot be vendored into an AGPL-3.0 repo.

sources.name: AcousticBrainz Genre Dataset (MediaEval)
sources.what: Genre ground truth from AllMusic, Discogs, Last.fm and Tagtraum joined to AcousticBrainz features. Discogs/Lastfm/Tagtraum are open; AllMusic needs a signed agreement. Licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — usable locally, not vendorable here.

sources.name: MUSDB18 / MedleyDB
sources.what: 150 and 122 tracks, stems corpora, academic use only, mostly CC BY-NC-SA. Too small, wrong shape (stems not masters), and licence-incompatible for vendoring. Reject for this purpose.

sources.name: iZotope Tonal Balance Control target curves
sources.what: 30+ genre/subgenre curves in v3 (12 in v2), built in-house from 'thousands of masters'. No numbers published anywhere; the curves live inside a proprietary plugin. Same for Har-Bal. Unusable as a reference source.

sources.name: MoSQITo (Eomys)
sources.what: Apache-2.0 (verified via the GitHub API), Python. Implements ISO 532-1 loudness and DIN 45692 sharpness with validation procedures. The nearest thing to a standardised proxy for 'bright/harsh', and licence-compatible with AGPL-3.0.

sources.name: ccMixter
sources.what: ~10k CC BY / CC BY-NC samples and tracks, free-form genre tags, no curated taxonomy. Fallback only.

options.name: Analytic EQ response only (what ships today)
options.how: crates/fxsound-dsp/tests/shipped_presets.rs already does this: impulse through GraphicEq, realfft, 29 third-octave points, pairwise worst-case dB difference. It proves distinctness and catches band summing.
options.breaks: Nothing — it is the current baseline. But it measures the EQ block alone. It never sees Dynamic Boost's auto-gain and −0.3 dBFS ceiling, the leveller, Bass, Ambience or Surround, all of which are program-dependent and none of which are bypassable. So what it measures is not what a listener gets.
options.why: Keep it. It answers 'are these twelve different from each other' and it answers it well. It cannot answer 'is Jazz jazz', and no extension of an impulse test can, because the stages that colour the result are nonlinear.

options.name: Genre-shaped synthetic program material through the FULL engine, scored as a 12×12 confusion matrix
options.how: New analysis module (reuse realfft 3.5.0, already a dep; no new runtime deps). Generate deterministic seeded material per genre: pink noise filtered to that genre's reference shape, plus a noise-burst train at a genre-typical crest factor to wake the dynamics stages. Render each of the 12 presets over each of the 12 materials through Engine::process at 48 kHz/1024-frame blocks. Measure: LTAS on the 29-point third-octave grid already in shipped_presets.rs, level-normalised to a shape (subtract the band mean); BS.1770-4 integrated LUFS (K-weighting is two biquads — biquad.rs exists); 4× oversampled true peak. Statistic: ΔD(P,g) = D(out,R_g) − D(in,R_g) after loudness-matching out to in, where D is weighted RMS dB error to the reference shape. The test asserts that for each genre column, the minimum of ΔD is the preset of that name, and reports the margin over the runner-up.
options.breaks: Nothing in the compatibility contract — no .fac file changes, no engine changes. It adds one data asset (12 × 29 floats) that must be regenerated if the reference method changes, and a test whose failure means 'this preset is not the best fit for its own genre', which will be uncomfortable the first time it runs.
options.why: This is the one that can be built and run today, entirely offline, in CI, in seconds, with no download and no licence question. And it is a genuinely stronger claim than the current tests: it exercises the whole nonlinear chain, and it is *relative*, so it survives the reference curve being only approximately right. Stationary noise under-exercises the transient behaviour — that is what the burst train is for, and it is still weaker than real music.

options.name: Render a real genre-labelled corpus (FMA) and measure the same ΔD over thousands of tracks
options.how: Filter fma_medium's tracks.csv (metadata CC BY 4.0) by `genre_top` and by the `license` column down to CC-BY / CC-BY-SA / CC0 tracks only. Decode outside the build with `ffmpeg -i x.mp3 -ac 2 -ar 48000 -f s16le -` piped to a new workspace member `crates/fxsound-voicing` (publish = false), so fxsound-dsp keeps its single dependency. Per track: render bypass and preset, loudness-match, compute ΔD, ΔLUFS, ΔPLR, clipped-sample count. Aggregate as median plus a bootstrap CI over tracks, and produce the 12×12 matrix plus docs/genre-voicing-measurement.{md,json} in the same style as the existing voice-presets research pair.
options.breaks: Nothing in the repo. Costs 22–93 GiB of download and hours of render. Never redistribute audio or renders — only derived numbers, with FMA's CC BY 4.0 attribution recorded. Coverage is the real break: FMA is indie/amateur CC material, not commercial masters, so it was mastered by different conventions than the Windows presets were voiced against.
options.why: The honest version of the test, and the only one where the material is real music. Run it once offline, check in the numbers, do not put it in CI. Note the coverage gaps up front: Metal and Trap are thin subgenres under Rock and Hip-Hop in FMA's 161-genre tree, and 70's / 80's are not genres at all — FMA has no era coverage, so those two presets are simply not testable by rendering.

options.name: Build the per-genre reference curves from AcousticBrainz barkbands (CC0, commercial masters)
options.how: Pull acousticbrainz-lowlevel-features-20220623-lowlevel.tar.zst (1 GB), take lowlevel.barkbands.mean (27 linear energies per track), convert to dB, normalise each track to a shape, join to genre by MBID using MusicBrainz's own CC0 genre/tag data (NOT the AcousticBrainz Genre Dataset, which is CC BY-NC-SA), and take per-genre medians plus percentile bands. Resample the 27 Bark centres onto the 29-point third-octave grid. Same join by release year gives era curves for the 70's / 80's presets.
options.breaks: Nothing. Two accuracy caveats that must be written down beside the numbers: the analyses were run by users on their own files of unknown encoding quality, and MusicExtractor applies replay gain, so absolute level is not comparable across tracks — which is exactly why every comparison in this proposal is shape-only and loudness-matched.
options.why: This is the answer to 'which genre reference spectra exist as numbers': none do, so make one. This is the only route to a reference built from *commercial* masters — the material the presets were actually voiced against — under a licence (CC0) that an AGPL repo can vendor without conditions. 27 Bark bands is coarser than 29 third-octaves and the resample is an approximation; say so in the asset header.

options.name: Vendor a published or commercial reference curve (Pestana/Reiss, Ozone Tonal Balance, Har-Bal)
options.how: Would mean lifting the AES paper's per-genre curves from figures, or extracting iZotope's or Har-Bal's targets from their binaries.
options.breaks: Licence, and accuracy. The AES per-genre curves exist only as plots behind a paywall; digitising a plot into a repo asset is both a rights problem and a precision problem. iZotope's 30+ curves and Har-Bal's are in-house, undocumented and embedded in proprietary plugins — extracting them into an AGPL-3.0 repo is not defensible.
options.why: There is exactly one usable number in this whole literature that is public: the ≈ −5 dB/octave decay from 100 Hz to 4 kHz, and it is a global curve across all popular music, not a per-genre one. Use it as a sanity check on a self-derived reference (does the derived curve slope roughly −5 dB/oct through the midband?) and nothing more.

options.name: Psychoacoustic proxies for the words that have no spectrum (sharpness, roughness, pumping, image width)
options.how: DIN 45692 sharpness in acum and ISO 532-1 loudness via MoSQITo (Apache-2.0, licence-compatible) as an offline Python check on rendered pairs; EBU R128 LRA and PLR from the LUFS code for leveller pumping; inter-channel correlation and a Gerzon energy-vector estimate for what Surround does to the image.
options.breaks: Nothing in the repo — these run on rendered output, offline. Implementing ISO 532-1 natively in Rust would be a large lift for little gain; call MoSQITo from a script instead.
options.why: Worth doing for the ceiling cases, and worth being blunt about what it buys. Sharpness in acum is a standardised measure of a signal property that correlates with the word 'bright' on stationary content. It is not a measure of whether a cymbal sounds harsh in a mix. Report the number, never let it decide.

options.name: Blind A/B harness — I cannot hear, but I can make the user's listening cheap and unbiased
options.how: A `--ab` mode on the measurement tool: take N tracks, render preset vs bypass (or preset vs preset), loudness-match to identical integrated LUFS, write them as randomly-ordered pairs into a folder with a hidden key file. The user listens, writes a choices file, the tool scores it against the key with a binomial p-value.
options.breaks: Nothing.
options.why: This is the direct answer to 'is there a way for you to listen': no, there is not, and there is no proxy that closes the gap. But loudness-matching and order-randomisation are exactly where informal listening goes wrong — a preset that is 2 dB louder wins every sighted comparison — and those are mechanical, so I can do them. Highest value per hour of anything in this list.

found.recommendation:
Build it in three layers, cheapest first.

**Layer 1 — an analysis module in the workspace, no new runtime deps, no downloads.** Add `ltas_thirds()` (Welch, Hann, 50% overlap, 8192-point realfft, power summed into the 29 third-octave centres already tabulated in `crates/fxsound-dsp/tests/shipped_presets.rs:167`), `lufs_integrated()` (BS.1770-4: K-weighting as two biquads on top of the existing `crates/fxsound-dsp/src/biquad.rs`, 400 ms blocks at 75% overlap, −70 LUFS absolute gate, −10 LU relative gate), `true_peak_dbtp()` (4× oversample), and PLR = true peak − integrated LUFS. Everything else in this proposal is built out of those four.

**Layer 2 — the falsifiable test, offline and in CI.** Check in `assets/reference/ltas-<genre>.csv`: 12 genres × 29 third-octave values, level-normalised to shapes, derived in Layer 3 and carrying a provenance header. Generate deterministic seeded program material per genre (pink noise shaped to that genre's reference, plus a noise-burst train at a genre-typical crest factor so the dynamics stages actually engage), render all 12 presets across all 12 materials through the real `Engine`, loudness-match output to input, and compute ΔD(P,g) = D(out,R_g) − D(in,R_g) where D is the weighted RMS dB error between level-normalised shapes over 40 Hz–16 kHz.

The test asserts one thing: **for each genre column, the preset whose ΔD is lowest is the preset of that name**, and it reports the margin over the runner-up. That claim is relative, so it holds up even when the reference curve is only approximately right — which it will be. Report, don't assert: ΔLUFS, ΔPLR, spectral centroid shift, clipped-sample count, and the spread of ΔD across materials. The whole matrix runs in seconds.

This is strictly stronger than what `shipped_presets.rs` can do today, because it sees Dynamic Boost's auto-gain and its −0.3 dBFS ceiling, the leveller, Bass, Ambience and Surround — none of which an impulse through `GraphicEq` ever touches, and none of which are bypassable.

**Layer 3 — the reference curves, derived once, offline.** There is no per-genre reference spectrum available as numbers anywhere: Pestana/Reiss is figures behind the AES paywall, iZotope's and Har-Bal's are proprietary and embedded, and the Million Song Dataset's 12 Echo Nest timbre coefficients are not invertible to a dB spectrum. So derive one. Primary: AcousticBrainz's `lowlevel.barkbands.mean` (27 Bark-band energies per track), CC0, ~29.5M tracks, 1 GB zstd, joined to genre and release year by MBID through MusicBrainz's own CC0 genre data — commercial masters, the material the presets were actually voiced against, under a licence this AGPL repo can vendor outright. Cross-check against a second reference derived by rendering licence-filtered FMA audio (metadata CC BY 4.0, per-track `license` column, decode via an external ffmpeg pipe so `fxsound-dsp` keeps its single dependency). Sanity-check both against the one public number in the literature: roughly −5 dB/octave from 100 Hz to 4 kHz.

**And Layer 0, which is the smallest and probably the most useful: the blind A/B harness.** I cannot hear the presets, and nothing above changes that. What I can do is remove the two things that make informal listening lie — render loudness-matched pairs at identical integrated LUFS, in randomised order, with a hidden key — and score the user's answers with a binomial test. Twelve presets, ten trials each, is an evening's work for a person who can hear, and it is the only step in this entire proposal that measures sound rather than a proxy for sound.

Build order: Layer 0 and Layer 1 first (both small, both immediately useful), then Layer 3's AcousticBrainz extraction, then Layer 2's test once there are curves to test against.
found.notes:
**What `process_wav.rs` can do today, and what it is missing.** It reads 16-bit PCM WAV only (it walks the chunk list properly, so real files with LIST/fact chunks work), applies a `.fac` preset or individual effect flags on the GUI's 0..10 scale, runs the real `Engine` in 1024-frame blocks exactly as an audio callback would, prints peak L/R from `engine.meters()` and a count of samples that exceeded full scale, and writes the result back. To render a corpus it needs: MP3/24-bit/float input (or an external ffmpeg pipe — cleaner, keeps `fxsound-dsp`'s single dependency intact), a bypass A/B render in one pass, LUFS and true-peak measurement, third-octave LTAS output, loudness-matching, and batch mode over a file list. None of that requires touching the engine.

**Three honest limits, stated plainly.**

*First, matching a genre reference proves 'not wrong', never 'right'.* A preset that lands exactly on the genre mean is average, and average is not what a preset is for — a preset is a deliberate colour. The strongest true statement this method can ever produce is: "the Jazz preset moves jazz-labelled material toward the jazz reference more than the other eleven presets do, by a margin of X dB with a CI of Y." That is a real claim and it is worth having. It is not "Jazz sounds like jazz".

*Second, the between-genre signal may be small and partly the wrong signal.* Elowsson & Friberg (AES 142, 2017) found that LTAS variation between genres is mainly a side-effect of percussive prominence. So a per-genre LTAS reference partly encodes "how much drums this genre has", not "how this genre should be EQ'd", and the between-genre spread is likely small against the within-genre spread. If the confusion matrix's diagonal margin falls inside its bootstrap CI, the correct conclusion is "these presets are provably distinct but not demonstrably genre-targeted" — and reporting that is a better outcome than a green test.

*Third, some judgements have no proxy at all.* "Does it sound harsh", "does the vocal sit right", "is that boost musical or resonant", "does the leveller pump", "does Surround widen or hollow it" — none of these are reachable. DIN 45692 sharpness, ECMA-418-2 roughness, EBU R128 LRA and inter-channel correlation each measure a signal property that correlates with one of those words on constrained material. They are worth computing and worth never letting decide anything.

**Repo-specific licence findings** (this repo is AGPL-3.0-or-later, `Cargo.toml:16`): AcousticBrainz data is CC0 — vendor freely. FMA metadata is CC BY 4.0 — vendorable with attribution; FMA audio is per-artist CC with a `license` column to filter on, and must never be redistributed, nor must renders of it. MTG-Jamendo metadata and the AcousticBrainz Genre Dataset are both CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — usable as local scratch, **not** vendorable into this repo. MUSDB18 and MedleyDB are academic-use-only stems corpora — reject on all three of size, shape and licence. MoSQITo is Apache-2.0 (verified via the GitHub API) and compatible.

**Two presets this cannot reach at all.** "70's" and "80's" are eras, not genres. No open corpus carries era-labelled renderable audio — FMA's release dates are upload dates for contemporary CC material. AcousticBrainz joined to MusicBrainz release years can give era *reference curves* (and era trend is precisely what the Pestana corpus was about), so those two presets can be checked against a curve but never by rendering era-appropriate material. Say so in the report rather than quietly testing them against something else.

**Structural suggestion:** follow the pattern already set by `docs/voice-presets-research.{md,json}` — a machine-readable JSON carrying every source, every derived number and every caveat, with a short human-readable MD beside it. The reference curves themselves belong in `assets/reference/` as CSV with a provenance header naming the dump date, the join, the track count per genre and the licence.
